data.hypothesis: The valid direct-global (32,8) candidate averaged 3.4738 µs versus the 3.5815 µs baseline, while (32,4) and (64,2) were slower. This experiment keeps one warp on adjacent X outputs at fixed Y/Z but uses a (32,16) block, reducing the grid from 1024 to 512 CTAs relative to (32,8). It tests whether fewer, larger CTAs help this small workload or instead increase resource pressure; no speedup is assumed.

memory_lessons.applicability: Relevant to the current direct-global stencil mapping comparison; these are three-sample measurements on the supplied workload, not confirmation of a general speedup.
memory_lessons.claim: The three valid direct-global candidates had mixed results: (32,8) averaged 3.4738 µs, (64,2) 3.5852 µs, and (32,4) 3.6217 µs. Their results suggest CTA/grid mapping remains worth testing, but do not establish the cause of the differences.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure the (32,16) mapping with the official full-run protocol and compare repeated results with baseline and the valid (32,8) candidate.

data.notes: The supplied baseline is valid at 3.5815 µs; prior candidates were also valid, with (32,8) the fastest measured at 3.4738 µs. This proposal has not been built or measured. The controller should validate varying signed inputs, including independent endpoint values, then measure repeated official full runs against baseline. No independent confirmation is available.
transformations: Replace the shared-memory stencil with one direct-global-load kernel producing one output per thread from all eight Y neighbors.
Use a (32,16,1) block and (2,4,64) grid: each warp covers adjacent X outputs at fixed Y/Z, with half as many CTAs as the previously measured (32,8) mapping.

Correct each neighbor coordinate with the specified add-63 / subtract-63 single-step rule, preserving in-range index 63; retain the supplied Y coefficients and do not modify inputs or read scratch contents.
